items.title: MIT study rules out wildfires, volcanoes as cause of recent surface warming

featured_image.name: Climate 'fingerprints' mark human activity from the top of the ...

items.description:
A team of MIT scientists has isolated the distinct global temperature effects of three landmark natural events — the 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo, the 2019-2020 Australian wildfires, and the 2022 Hunga Tonga underwater volcanic eruption — using decades of satellite data and a novel signal-to-noise approach, according to a study published this week in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.[1][2]

The findings show that while all three events left measurable marks on atmospheric temperatures, none appear to explain the accelerating warming trend at Earth's surface in recent years, pointing instead to human activity as the dominant driver.[3][1]

items.title: Bitcoin drops below $63,000 as Trump's 15% tariff takes effect

featured_image.name: Trump tariffs live updates: Trump raises 'global' tariff to 15%; US to stop collecting duties deemed illegal

items.description:
Bitcoin tumbled more than 5% on Tuesday, sliding below $63,000 as a new round of global tariffs took effect and escalating tensions in the Middle East pushed investors further away from risk assets. The leading cryptocurrency fell to a low of $62,964.64, according to CNBC, as market participants engaged in what analysts described as broad "tactical de-risking."[1]

The drop coincided with the midnight implementation of President Donald Trump's 15% global import tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 — a statute never before invoked by a president. Trump signed the measure on February 20, initially setting the rate at 10%, before raising it to the statutory maximum of 15% the following day via a post on Truth Social. The move came just hours after the U.S. Supreme Court, in a 6-3 ruling in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, struck down the administration's previous tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.[2][3][4][5][6][7]

items.title: Oil prices near 7-month highs as U.S.-Iran talks loom

featured_image.name: Oil hovers below seven-month high as traders eye U.S.–Iran talks ...

items.description:
Oil prices hovered near seven-month highs on Tuesday as traders weighed the prospect of a new round of U.S.-Iran nuclear talks against an increasingly bellicose tone from President Donald Trump, who warned Tehran of a "very bad day" if negotiations fail.

Brent crude futures rose 0.8% to $72.08 a barrel in early Asian trade on Tuesday, nearing their highest level since late July, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude climbed 0.9% to $66.88 a barrel. Both benchmarks had touched their firmest levels in roughly seven months during Monday's session, with Brent reaching $72.50 and WTI hitting $67.28, before pulling back.[1][2][3]

items.title: Rival studies clash over fate of massive dying star WOH G64

featured_image.name: SALT solves stellar mystery: WOH G64 still alive as a red ...

items.description:
WOH G64, one of the most extreme stars ever observed, is at the center of a scientific debate over whether it is on a path toward imminent destruction or simply behaving strangely under the influence of a companion star.

A study published February 23 in Nature Astronomy by a team led by Gonzalo Muñoz-Sanchez concludes that WOH G64 has undergone a "dramatic transition" from a red supergiant to a yellow hypergiant, a rare and unstable phase that can precede a supernova explosion. The researchers analyzed more than three decades of photometric and spectroscopic data, finding that the star's effective temperature increased by more than 1,000 degrees Kelvin since roughly 2014. They describe WOH G64 as a "rare, massive symbiotic binary system" and propose that the transition could result from the partial ejection of its outer envelope or the winding down of a decades-long eruption.[1][2][3]

items.title: Explosion near Moscow train station kills police officer on Ukraine war anniversary

featured_image.name: Man kills police officer in Moscow train station blast

items.description:
An unidentified assailant detonated an explosive device beside a police patrol vehicle at Savyolovsky Station Square in central Moscow early Tuesday, killing himself and a traffic police officer and wounding two others, Russian authorities said. The blast came just minutes into February 24 — the fourth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The attack occurred at approximately 00:05 Moscow time, according to Moscow's branch of the Interior Ministry, which said the man approached officers sitting inside a patrol car before the device went off. One officer was killed instantly, while two others were hospitalized.[1][2][3][4][5]

items.title: Ukraine reconstruction costs hit $588B as war marks four years

featured_image.name: Russia hits power stations after Ukraine counter-offensive

items.description:
As Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine enters its fifth year on February 24, 2026, UN Secretary-General António Guterres called the war "a stain on our collective consciousness" and renewed his demand for "an immediate, full and unconditional ceasefire" as a first step toward lasting peace. In remarks to the Human Rights Council on Monday, Guterres noted that more than 15,000 civilians have been killed and declared: "It is more than past time to end the bloodshed".[1][2][3][4]

The anniversary comes days after the latest round of US-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine ended without a breakthrough in Geneva, where negotiations on territorial control and security guarantees remain at an impasse.[5][6]

items.title: Russian oil exports top prewar levels despite four years of sanctions

featured_image.name: Russia's crude exports slump to the lowest in 11 months

items.description:
Four years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the volume of Russian crude oil being shipped abroad remains above prewar levels, even as the revenue Moscow earns from those barrels has fallen sharply, according to new data published on the fourth anniversary of the conflict.

The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, a Finland-based think tank known as CREA, reported on Tuesday that Russian crude oil export volumes in the 12 months ending February 24, 2026, remained six percent above pre-invasion levels, totaling 215 million tonnes. Yet revenues from those crude exports dropped 18 percent year-on-year to 85.5 billion euros, as Russia has been forced to sell at steep discounts to attract buyers. Total fossil fuel export revenues fell to an estimated 193 billion euros for the period, down 27 percent from comparable pre-invasion levels.[1][2][3][4][5]

items.title: EU leaders visit Kyiv as Ukraine marks four years of war

featured_image.name: Ukraine marks four years since Russian invasion - Yahoo

items.description:
On Tuesday, February 24, 2026 — exactly four years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion — Ukraine entered a fifth year of fighting with no end in sight, as its people continue to endure daily bombardment, displacement, and an energy crisis that has left millions shivering through one of the harshest winters in recent memory.

Senior European Union leaders traveled to Kyiv to mark the occasion. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa attended an official memorial ceremony, visited energy infrastructure damaged by Russian missile strikes, and held a trilateral meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. The Coalition of the Willing, a group of 35 countries convened by British Prime Minister Keir Starmer and French President Emmanuel Macron, held a videoconference reaffirming support for Ukraine. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte participated in a separate ceremony at NATO headquarters in Brussels.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: 2026 is deadliest start to a year for Mediterranean migrants, UN says

featured_image.name: Migrant boat docks in Crete after dramatic rescue

items.description:
The United Nations' International Organization for Migration announced Monday that at least 606 migrants have died or gone missing in the Mediterranean Sea since the beginning of 2026, making it the deadliest start to a year since the agency began tracking such data in 2014.[1][2][3]

The grim milestone came as search operations continued off the Greek island of Crete, where a vessel carrying roughly 50 people capsized on Saturday approximately 20 nautical miles south of the port of Kali Limenes. Twenty people were rescued, including four minors, and the bodies of three men and one woman were recovered, according to the Associated Press. About 30 others remain unaccounted for.[4][1]
